replacement: The second region has a more varied surface and is better suited to human habitation. Two long chains of mountains divide it from one end to the other. The Alleghany ridge follows the shape of the Atlantic coast, and the other chain runs parallel to the Pacific. The space between these two chains covers 1,341,649 square miles. *a Its area is therefore about six times that of France. Yet this vast territory forms a single valley. One side descends gradually from the rounded summits of the Alleghanies, while the other rises in an unbroken slope toward the tops of the Rocky Mountains. At the bottom of the valley flows an immense river, which receives the streams coming down from the mountains on every side. In memory of their homeland, the French once called this river the St. Louis. The Native Americans, in their pompous language, named it the Father of Waters, the Mississippi.

The valley watered by the Mississippi seems to have been shaped to be the bed of this mighty river, which, like a god of antiquity, dispenses both good and evil along its course. On the banks of the stream, nature shows an inexhaustible fertility. As you move away from the banks, the power of growth weakens, the soil becomes poor, and the plants that survive grow sickly. Nowhere have the great upheavals of the globe left clearer traces than in the valley of the Mississippi. The whole look of the country shows the powerful effects of water, in its fertility as well as in its barrenness. The waters of the primeval ocean piled up enormous beds of rich soil in the valley, and leveled them as they drew back. On the right bank of the river, one sees immense plains as smooth as if a farmer had gone over them with a roller. As you approach the mountains, the ground becomes steadily more uneven and barren. In a thousand places it is pierced by primitive rocks, which look like the bones of a skeleton whose flesh has partly wasted away. The surface of the earth is covered with granite sand and huge, irregular masses of stone. A few plants force their way up among them, and the whole looks like a green field strewn with the ruins of a vast building. On examination, these stones and this sand prove to be perfectly analogous to those that make up the dry, broken summits of the Rocky Mountains. The flood that washed the soil down to the bottom of the valley later carried off pieces of the rocks themselves. These were dashed and battered against the neighboring cliffs, and were left scattered like wrecks at their feet. *d On the whole, the valley of the Mississippi is the most magnificent dwelling place that God has prepared for man; and yet at present it can be called only a mighty desert.

replacement: These immense deserts were not, however, without human inhabitants. Some wandering tribes had lived for ages scattered among the forest shades or the green pastures of the prairie. From the mouth of the St. Lawrence to the delta of the Mississippi, and from the Atlantic to the Pacific Ocean, these savages shared certain resemblances that bore witness to a common origin. At the same time they differed from all other known races of men. *g They were neither white like the Europeans, nor yellow like most Asians, nor black, as Black people are. Their skin was reddish brown, their hair long and shining, their lips thin, and their cheekbones very prominent. The languages of the North American tribes differed in their words, but they followed the same grammatical rules. In several respects these rules differed from the ones that had been observed to govern the origin of language elsewhere. The speech of the Native Americans seemed to be the product of new combinations, and it showed an effort of the understanding of which the Native Americans of our own day would be incapable. *h

replacement: The social state of these tribes also differed in many respects from anything seen in the Old World. They seemed to have multiplied freely in the midst of their deserts, without coming into contact with other races more civilized than themselves. Accordingly, they showed none of those vague and confused notions of right and wrong, and none of that deep corruption of customs, which usually go together with ignorance and crudeness in nations that have advanced to civilization and then fallen back into barbarism. The Native American owed nothing to anyone but himself. His virtues, his vices, and his prejudices were his own work. He had grown up in the wild independence of his nature.
